Opacity never rides a spring, and the single curve token splits in two because a page may overshoot where a toast may not.

**Adopting apps:** `--motion-curve` becomes `--motion-page-ease`, plus `--motion-toast-ease` for the toast. Take opacity out of `glim-page-in` and `glim-toast-in` and pair each with `glim-fade-in` on `ease-out`, or give the whole animation a curve that does not spring. Both satisfy the rule; the second is what a numerous element needs.

## 🎨 Design

- **Opacity never rides a spring.** A spring has a control point past 1, so it drives its value through the target and back. For a distance that is the point; for opacity it is meaningless, because the value clamps at 1. The fade finishes early and then sits flat, so the dial set to make an entrance longer makes its fade shorter. Movement takes the level's curve, the fade takes one that only eases.
- **It was found the hard way, and it is the one part of that report with an answer.** An adopting app's top motion level flashed a flat green badge on Firefox/macOS. Two releases chased mechanisms inferred from reading the stylesheet and neither helped. What settled it was a four-panel test file walking the change that introduced the spring: with opacity taken off it, the reporter said that panel looked clean. An alpha driven past 1 into a premultiplied software rasteriser is the shape of that defect, and the page's own CSS never named the colour.
- **Two shapes satisfy the rule, and choosing between them is measured rather than a matter of taste.** A transform-only keyframe paired with `glim-fade-in` is tidier. Keeping the fade in the keyframe and dropping the springing curve is what a NUMEROUS element needs: a two-animation shorthand costs real parse time, and 66 staggered rows took an adopting app's test from passing to 8.8s against a 5s budget. Guard the invariant, never one of the shapes, or the expensive one gets forced everywhere.
- **A page may spring where a toast may not.** A page arriving is free to overshoot. A toast slides in from the screen edge, and a spring carries it back past the edge it came from, which reads as a glitch. They agree again at `storm`, where restraint is the thing being switched off.

## 🐛 Fixed

- **`glim-page-in` and `glim-toast-in` animated opacity on the per-level curve**, so both carried the defect above at the two levels whose curves spring.
- **The quiet levels do not name a toast curve**, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: a level asking for less movement is not asking for a different easing, and the shorter duration carries the change. A livelier level has no such excuse, which is why `storm` names both.
